For this source, when there are more data, such as on urban roads, the two data sets are in better agreement. For single-unit short-haul, we observe FleetDNA trucks driving about 4%–6% more on weekdays compared to MOVES for urban roads, but both spend near three-quarters of total driving on weekdays. For refuse trucks, CE-CERT shows high weekday driving proportions, which may be indicative of California- specific trash pickup days. Finally, for transit buses, we see good agreement on urban other roads between the two data sets, but FleetDNA transit buses do more weekday driving on urban freeways than CE-CERT buses. For the combined data columns, the shading does not arise from the hourly data density section, but from our recommendations; gray indicates data that are not recommended for incorporation into MOVES, orange for categories that we do not recommend for updating MOVES despite the large sample size of vehicles, and no shading for categories recommended for updating MOVES. An anomaly, combination-unit long-haul, has enough data in terms of sample size at 70 vehicles, but the three fleets comprising it may not have typical weekday vs. weekend driving and thus have been shaded orange. Because this was an unexpected result and the three fleets may have had incentives to drive more on the weekend and thus not be representative of nationwide combination-unit long-haul driving, we do not recommend these distributions to update MOVES, and that selection is reflected in Section 6: Conclusions. However, this could indicate a growing trend for long-haul truck behavior, and those interested in fleet driving patterns may want to watch for a continuation of this pattern with new data. Combination-unit short-haul vehicles on rural roads have no shading, in contrast to the data density section due to the higher level of aggregation on day VMT fractions with 26 and 27 vehicles and 202 and 38 hours logged on rural freeways and other roads, respectively. However, if viewed as an improvement over MOVES, non-source-specific day-type distributions could be incorporated even with non- robust data. The school bus exception has been discussed previously; we would not typically think that a sample size of four buses constitutes enough data, but we deem these four school buses more representative of school bus behavior than many other heavy-duty trucks lacking school operation. Other bus operations are solely from five airport shuttles and may not be representative of the source type as a whole, and as such these are not recommended for use in MOVES.
